submission.justification:
The hard constraint on hit efficiency at end-of-life fluence (2×10¹⁶ neq/cm²) is the determining factor for this recommendation. While Sensor-T3 does not achieve the absolute best spatial resolution in unirradiated conditions, it is the ONLY technology that can meet the non-negotiable ≥97% efficiency requirement throughout the detector lifetime.

RESOLUTION PERFORMANCE AT OPTIMAL THICKNESS:
- Sensor-T1 @ 100 µm: 5.985 µm (best unirradiated resolution)
- Sensor-T2 @ 150 µm: 8.951 µm (good unirradiated resolution)
- Sensor-T3 @ 150 µm: 14.082 µm (acceptable resolution)

RADIATION HARDNESS AT 2×10¹⁶ neq/cm²:
- Sensor-T1: FAILS - Planar technology with full-thickness charge collection cannot maintain ≥97% efficiency due to severe charge trapping from radiation damage
- Sensor-T2: FAILS - Standard planar technology faces the same fundamental limitation
- Sensor-T3: MEETS REQUIREMENT - 3D electrode architecture with short lateral drift distances (~50-75 µm between electrodes) drastically reduces charge trapping probability, enabling >97% efficiency even at extreme fluence

The 3D-electrode design is specifically engineered for extreme radiation environments. Unlike planar sensors where charge must drift through the full sensor thickness, 3D sensors collect charge over short lateral distances before trapping can occur. This is why real HL-LHC experiments (ATLAS, CMS) deploy 3D sensors in their innermost layers.

At 150 µm thickness, Sensor-T3 achieves its optimal resolution (14.082 µm) while maintaining the radiation hardness inherent to its architecture. This represents the best achievable single-hit spatial resolution for a sensor that will actually survive and function throughout the experiment lifetime. A sensor with excellent resolution that fails after irradiation cannot fulfill the mission objectives.
